idiom_name: state-owning wrapper + stateless children (values down, events up)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each subtree exactly one explicit owner of state and data access - the wrapper creates or subscribes to the source, performs the side effects, and renders its children with values plus callbacks. Children stay pure: same input, same output, no knowledge of where the data came from and no subscriptions of their own. Treat the two lifecycles separately - set up and release the subscription in the wrapper's lifecycle hook, and keep every child renderable from a plain data literal. Where the platform supplies bindings, signals, session state or template locals, use that mechanism instead of hand-rolled prop plumbing; where it does not, hand-write the same split as a state owner plus render functions that stay disconnected from the source. Keep the container's fetch scope tight: pass each child only the slice of the snapshot it actually reads, not the whole object. Use a typed contract (interface, protocol, type) for the props so drift between container and child is a compile-time rather than runtime error.
code_sketch:
# container: owns the state and the source
state = source.subscribe()                     # or fetch/derive once
def render(children):
    return child(view=state.value, on_event=state.handle)   # values down

# child: stateless, no source access
def child(view, on_event):
    return markup(view)                        # events up
pitfalls: Letting a child reach into the source directly recreates the coupling the split removes.
Owning state too high re-renders the whole subtree; keep local UI state in the leaf that reads it.
Forgetting to release the wrapper's subscription when the component goes away leaks listeners.
Over-fetching and passing a full snapshot forces children to re-render on every field change even if they only read one.
Prop drilling through the container to grandchildren indicates the container scope is too wide or the tree needs a context provider.
Handling loading, error and empty states inside the child instead of the container leaks branching logic into the reusable layer.

Wrong move: enforcing the smart/dumb split as a hard rule, one container per component -> the pattern's own author stopped endorsing the dogma and the codebase fills with wrapper files for logic a single hook could expose -> instead treat the split as a guideline and extract world-aware logic into a custom hook, or one wrapper only where reuse across sources is real.

Wrong move: one root container issuing a single giant query for the whole page -> responses are delayed, cache reuse suffers and every child re-renders on unrelated field changes -> instead colocate each view's data requirements with that view (fragments or per-component queries) and compose them at the edge.

Wrong move: keeping dedicated container files after the framework ships a hook that does the same job (useSelector, useFragment, ComponentStore) -> the wrapper layer becomes ceremony that hides where the state lives -> instead migrate the separation into the hook and keep a container only where the same view truly serves multiple sources.
